utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you continue, just to note that we are in receipt of a filing from the head of the interpretation unit with regard to that disputed passage and its interpretation, and the English transcript should be corrected to read: "All the people who are members of the KLA would open fire from the fortifications in the direction of the police." I believe you would have received that. Mr. Milosevic is to be thanked for his intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, I was dealing with death in custody yesterday, and I'm going to continue with that theme for a short while. Kacanik was also an area broadly within your interest, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, what I can tell you is that the Kacanik area is an area that I have much fewer information than for the Stimlje area, because in Kacanik area it was peaceful practically until --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And therefore I have fewer information concerning this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm cross-examining from a document to be found in volume 2 your materials at tab 9, page 9 of 17. Do you remember an incident in mid-1998 when, in fact, it was Serb policemen who killed another Serb policeman in the Kacanik area? Policemen concerned who did the killing were Ljubisa Boskovic and Slobodan Jankovic. So it was Serb on Serb. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's not true that one Serb policeman killed another Serb policeman. As far as I can remember, that case took place in a village. I can't remember the name of the village right now. I remember that it was a criminal offence from Article 125 of the Criminal Code of the then Yugoslavia. It was the criminal offence of terrorism. Ljubisa Boskovic is somebody I know. I think he was assistant commander in the Kacanik organ of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how, then, if he wasn't the killer does he feature in this case? How do you know what case I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that case while back in Urosevac, and I know for a fact that he was not the killer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. How does he feature in the case at all? I've asked you about a killing of Serb on Serb. I suggested there was a killing by Ljubisa Boskovic. You know the killing. You say he wasn't involved. What killing was I referring to? You see --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You told me yourself that a Serb policeman killed another Serb policeman. I don't remember such a case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then how can you connect it with --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Boskovic? Come on, help us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You yourself mentioned that he was killed by Ljubisa Boskovic. You mentioned his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ljubisa Boskovic did do the killing, did he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I'm telling you -- I'm stating with full responsibility that it is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very helpful, Mr. Jasovic, and I'm going to put my last question in this way: There was a case of Serb killing Serb. Danica Marinkovic got involved and said the thing should be dealt with as if it was an act of terrorism by the KLA. That's the way it was hushed up, and this accused sent a telegram along with other dignitaries praising the deceased policeman for his bravery. And that's the way things were in Kosovo in mid-1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true, Mr. Nice. I apologise. I feel quite uncomfortable in having to say this, but you keep putting questions to me that are outside of the scope of my work. I can tell you about things based on the documents that I have. I cannot answer questions on behalf of the Urosevac SUP or the chief of the criminal investigation department because that's persons were involved in handling all of the matters in the jurisdiction of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, what was the name of the Serb policeman who was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you frankly I can't remember his name. I just can't. It's been seven years. That was in 1998, and it's 2005 now. So it's been seven years, and I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving to tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the exhibit number or the document number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's document 9, and the history can be seen at page -- I think I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is 9 in volume 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 9 in volume 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it can be found at page 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can then go to tab 10, another person who had direct contact with events at the time, SS376 as he is known. And on page 11 of this document. Sorry, page 12, paragraph 64. This potential witness came to your police station where a body was being removed in about 1993 or 1994, and on that occasion found a body who was said to have committed suicide by jumping from the fourth-floor window. Do you remember anything about that, an alleged suicide from the fourth-floor window in 1993 or 1994.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I feel quite uncomfortable again, but I have to tell you, I have to reiterate that I do not remember that case. On the fourth floor were the offices of the members of the state security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's quite a big police station. Let's have a look at a picture of it. It's quite a big station so we can have an idea of what it looks like look. The overhead projector doesn't need to be produced. But it gives us an idea of the scale of the building. This is the building where you work. Now, the fourth floor we can see, and the third floor we can see. And we can see the scale of the enterprise, but if prisoners or people detained are alleged to have committed suicide from the fourth floor window it's not a usual -- at least I hope it's not a usual event, Mr. Jasovic. Presumably it's a matter of concern to a police force. Now, do you have no recollection of any prisoner dying in or from custody at this police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember. I'm stating with full responsibility this. You told me that he had jumped off the fourth floor. I'm claiming with full responsibility that I do not remember the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying he jumped off the fourth floor. I'm saying that the cover story was that he committed suicide from the fourth floor, and I'm asking for your help with what actually happened. Can you help?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if I remembered this, I would have told you. However, I do not remember, and I feel quite uncomfortable about not remembering. I wasn't involved in this case, and I do not remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 11, then, please, K56. And on this document, this is another of your colleagues. First of all, is he -- is this colleague of yours right at paragraph 25 in saying that official police documents were burned before you decamped from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say what pertains to my internal documentation that has to do with terrorism cases. This is what I brought with me, and I don't know what happened to the rest of documentation. There were various fields of work, investigation, search, homicide, sexual offences, and so on. So I couldn't tell you anything about this issue. The head of the organ would probably be able to tell you. I really didn't follow this issue, whether this had been burned or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to move on from that to 1998. There's a document that I'll just lay on the overhead projector. I only have one copy of it. It's a report, if we can read it in English, from the Humanitarian Law Centre in 1998, and it deals extensively with police violence and brutality, but let's just read two passages and see if something as recent as 1998 is in your recollection. It says here that somebody called Rexhep Bislimi, a Human Rights activist and former prisoner of conscience, died at Pristina hospital on the 21st of July, he having on the 3rd of July been the subject of a district prosecutor request to investigate on charges of seditious conspiracy. He was arrests in Urosevac on the 6th of July, taken to the prison in Gnjilane, transferred to the hospital. His body was covered with bruises. His arm was broken. Photographs were taken. And three ribs were fractured. So he died from a beating, it appears, in the police station. Do you know anything about Rexhep Bislimi?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the person Rexhep Bislimi. I don't understand what was said in English, but you said that the person was sent on to the district prison in Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want to say that the district prison killed him? By all means do if that's the reality.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I want to say. No, no, no. I don't know whether this person was killed. But if we're talking about Gnjilane, members of the state security in Urosevac came under the security services centre in Gnjilane. What I'm trying to say is that the operations officers of the state security in Gnjilane most likely worked with these persons. I don't remember any Rexhep Bislimi, and I don't know what to tell you and I feel uncomfortable once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer. I wasn't kept abreast. I didn't take part in that work. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of which we've seen a picture it was possible for these terrible things to be happening that I've recounted to you and you not to know about it? Is that what you're you going?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know that in the police station in Urosevac terror was used or violence or that there were people who were killed there. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next part of this report that relates specifically to your police station is at the bottom of the page and it says this: "According to the Prizren branch of the Kosovo Committee for the Protection of Human Rights, Maksut Caflesi from Belobrade village died on 23rd of August after being tortured by police in Urosevac. His brother stated that Caflesi was stopped and beaten by police on the Prizren-Urosevac road. He received no medical attention in Urosevac and was subsequently transferred to the Pristina hospital where he died." The report goes on: "Biljal Salja, a 47-year-old teacher and member of the ethnic Albanian Social Democratic Party, died at Urosevac police station on the 29th of August. He was arrested on the 28th of August together with his son Agron, who was released later that day. Agron heard had I father's cries when the police interrogated him. On the 30th of August the family was notified that they could take over Salja's body from the Pristina hospital morgue." Right. What's your state of recollection about those two deaths in custody?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not interview these two persons, and I'm telling you frankly I don't remember any of those two cases. Neither do I remember that they were dead at the police station in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember these cases, Mr. Jasovic, and it maybe you were the officer involved and you're uncomfortable --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, no. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're uncomfortable --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I'm uncomfortable. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, we have it again available --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee that you can go in and verify. I was not involved in any of those cases, neither in these ones that you mention nor in the previous ones, and I'm stating this very firmly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, how many prisoners could the -- or can the Urosevac police station hold at any one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I entered the detention room only twice way back when I was the assistant commander of the police station. So I don't really know that room, and I couldn't tell you whether it was two by three or two by four metres. I really can't remember because it was back in 1980 something when I entered that room only twice. I'm telling you the truth. There's no reason for me to conceal anything. Whether it was two by three metres, I don't know. It was a detention room across from the office in the secretariat premises, and I couldn't tell you whether 20 or 30 persons could fit in. I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's the detention room where persons would be held.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. It's a detention room in -- on the ground floor. As I said, across from the office of the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You don't know the size of the detention room at your police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't really tell you. I don't know the exact dimensions, the width and the length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Jasovic, by 1998 the police state that you were operating was one in which you had impunity. You could act without fear of consequence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I acted in accordance with the law. I'm a professional, and I have a status of an authorised official. So it's not true that I would be afraid had I used violence, terror, had I overstepped my authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law was the same for me and for other colleagues of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only were you -- I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, did you ever arrest anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not take part in operations. I never took somebody into custody or arrested somebody. I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only were you a violent man but by 1998 and thereabouts you had become committed. Your former colleague - tab 9, page 7 of 17, paragraph 25 - describes how you would take people's passports away in the interests of the Serbs. Do you remember doing that? Taking passports away from people to stop them travelling?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. That's not true. Persons who were taken into custody or persons who came in to provide information voluntarily would not usually come in with their passports. I did not go out in the field or stop people in the streets to take their passports or their documents away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you locate the passage again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. It's tab 9, and it's at paragraph -- page 17, I think I said -- well, that must be wrong because there's only 16 pages. It was indeed page 7, paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, another way in which you showed your political commitment was your distress at people buying land from Serbs, at Albanians buying land from Serbs. Do you remember -- remember having anxiety or distress about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that I was distressed. What I can say about this is that there was the law limiting the sale of real property that provided that if a number of Serbs, residents of one street or so on, wrote a petition, certain measures had to be taken in keeping with the law, and I think that there was also a misdemeanour set forth there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you got involved in those offences, did you? Despite really being interested in terrorism, you did get yourself involved in misdemeanours concerning land sale, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally was not involved in misdemeanours. Criminal complaints or misdemeanours are generally filed by police members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must move on. Tab 12 of the same volume of materials, and Dr. Xhela Recica who we referred to yesterday. Were you aware that this doctor was being a record of those who were tortured in your police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday or the day before yesterday that I don't know that physician, although I do know a lot of Albanian doctors. However, do I not know him, and I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you'd like please to have -- the Court would like to very swiftly cast its eye over, first of all, the page that begins on the top right-hand corner K0505383, which is the notes he made. If you could just make that available to the witness. Mr. Nort, coming your way. Lay this on the overhead projector, please. You see, this doctor, as from 1991, kept carefully in Latin records of people who came to his practice, he having been thrown out of his job as a doctor earlier. Do you know anything about this doctor at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said already that although I know quite a few Albanian doctors, I don't know his name and surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... eye down the name -- just do it for 1991 and then we'll do it for 1998. Just cast your eyes down --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be fair to the witness to show him documents in a language he understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, this is not -- where is this from?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The doctor kept records in Latin about injuries suffered by people coming to him complaining of what they'd received at the police station. No, we haven't translated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO and it will have to be sufficient --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- interpreters translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did they not write in hand? It's not a handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He kept it on computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He converted it to a computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Converted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't remember the details of what he said about that, but it was certainly written in hand and then stored in typed form, yes. He made up a logbook. We can find that in his statement which comes before it. It's paragraphs 9 and 10 of the statement at page 3. "I wrote the diagnosis in Latin," paragraph 9, "I recorded such detail on a protected sure file on my computer. I would write a report on the patient visit, describe his injuries, diagnosis and treatment, and I would add in more details about how they described to me how they received their injuries." This is part of his record. I was going --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, if you'd look please at the document on the screen, all I want you to do, please, is to cast your eyes down the names which you will be able to read, starting with Behxhet Hyseni, then going to Milazim Murati, Afrim Xhafaj, Ahmet Hoxha, and so on. Just tell us, do you remember dealing with any of these people -- it's a long time, 1991, but I just wondered if you'd just like to see if any of these names are familiar to you and then we'll go and do the same thing for 1998, reflecting that there are continuous entries throughout the time. Any of those names familiar to you? Any?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the names. I cannot remember the names. It's 1991, as you say. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on what grounds they were perhaps brought to the SUP. I'm saying perhaps. I don't know. I don't know whether this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... good enough to turn on to what is on the foot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the diagnosis in relation to, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Various. And my Latin is of very indifferent quality, but you can get it if necessary. But you can see various descriptions of abrasions, bruising, I think, contusions, and it may be fractures as well. We haven't had them all translated. Time doesn't permit. But they are complaints coming from Ferizaj police station, for the most part or all. And if Mr. Nort would be good enough to turn to what is at the foot of the page, page 28, we'll see the first there, and I'll only bother with the first of I think it's eight pages and a total of -- a total of 83 people complaining in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But perhaps if you'd be good enough when page 28 is there - thank you very much - just run your eyes down the first 14 names of people who complained of mistreatment at your police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All of them seem to be contusion on the head and body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you see let's just run down these names Nijazi Kadri Shabani, Hyzri Beqir Sejdiu, Xhevat Abdullah Raci, et cetera. Keep your eye down the page. Any you can help us with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what basis is this medical report linked to the police station? I don't understand that. People go to doctors for various reasons. On the basis of what does Mr. Nice claim today in 2005 that these people had been at the police station and beaten there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's asking the witness this question, and if the witness can answer, perhaps a connection within established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it would help the accused, and if when he has the time to do so, but he's had this file to help him over the weekend, since last week, he's had it over a week, if he goes back and consults the statement of the doctor at the beginning of this tab he'll find the answer to his concerns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any names that you recognise there, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I cannot remember these names. I cannot. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go on, then, in -- I'm going to come back to the doctor at a later stage where his materials are more easily dealt with, but I want to deal very briefly with some other materials we have about you, Mr. Jasovic, and these are statements of a different kind. First of all, tab 13, Your Honours. In fact, I'm not even sure I need trouble with tab 13. Oh, yes. No, I must deal with tab 13. Were you aware that there was a man called Ruzhdi Jashari? Do you know that man's name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person Ruzhdi Jashari is someone I do not know personally except that I know that he keeps being mentioned in the statements as a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also a member of -- well, whether he's mentioned in the statements or not, I don't know. But he's also a member of the Council of Human Rights and Freedoms.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of that. I think he was a journalist, too, some correspondent of some paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, people came to him with their own handwritten complaints. And with Mr. Nort's assistance we'll turn in this tab to top right-hand corner page 505193. This is in tab 13, Mr. Nort. Rapidly, please, if you could, 505193. There is an original handwritten version of this lying behind it, but just hand this to the -- Mr. Nort, if you would just hand this please -- no. 515 -- 93. Sorry. 5193. And can you hand this to the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 64 is before 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not filed in an orderly manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think paginating of typed document and handwritten document go --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that was handed in, handwritten by the person concerned, bearing the date the 8th of June of 1998, and it says this: "At 1030," he deals with his, the circumstances of his detention which were brutal. But then he says: "At 1030 they took me and another man, six of us, aged 20 to 25, to the police station in Ferizaj. There they have beaten us brutally like animals until they got us inside the facility." He lists the various people who were detained. "They asked us," he goes on, "do we know who killed the policemen?" There was a policeman who had been killed. In the end they took our personal data and said that we should give our weapons in by Saturday." "To me personally," he says, "they injured my left eye, bleeding in my jaw and my rib. My wife has injuries to her head." And we see the name of the man at the top, Mehdi Sopaj. An example of somebody who writes his own complaint in 1998 and hands it into the Council for Human Rights. Do you have any recollection of Mehdi Sopaj being dealt with like this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The person did not come for an interview to see me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go on a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, on which floor of the police office was your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the third floor, number 59. The third floor, number 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, will you be seeking to call any of these informants in your rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In rebuttal I will be seeking to call, if necessary, the producers of statements, and if the ruling of the Court is it has to be also not just the same level of hearsay as may be allowed at the moment to the accused, then I'll, if necessary, call the complainants themselves. They're alive. I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm beginning to form a view about the importance of these statements if we are to be able to form a view, an accurate view of the entire issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These people will all be available, and I've only got one more in this connection -- this is of people. If Mr. Nort could go on and find a page which is 5196.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us just -- let us just clarify one thing, Mr. Robinson. These are not even second -- this is not even secondhand evidence. This is thirdhand evidence, statements. This is: "[In English] Complained in my presence and I certify the documents and I give to investigator Kelly are true copies of the original statement." [Interpretation] So he gives a statement that some Albanians had given statements to him, and Mr. Nice is bringing that in now as evidence without witnesses, without making statements, without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I wasn't inviting an argument on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I only make this comment, not to be thought difficult but just to alert the accused to where we stand, the level of hearsay is identical with the level of hearsay when Danica Marinkovic introduced via the medium of this witness statements of other people. So it's the same level of hearsay. If you'd like to take out the page that follows this, Mr. Nort, and make that available to the witness and we'll read the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, Mr. Jasovic, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you have another objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In relation to the mention of Mrs. Marinkovic now. Danica Marinkovic, investigating judge, explained here that she took statements in the presence of the public prosecutor, the accused or, rather, the suspect and the lawyer of the suspect concerned. So if that is at the same level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. This is not the time to debate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at this statement, this is somebody who came back to the Council for Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Suva Reka from the village of Laniste wanting to add to an earlier statement that he'd given. And he said this: "During the time I was in the improvised prison, in a private house in Ferizaj which was close to the technical school," where he was held as a hostage, he experienced inhuman tortures that the Serbian police and military used. "They used the most barbarian means, including electric shock, with one and only one intention ..." This comes from a man called Osman Halili. Now, do you remember Osman Halili?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't remember this person. But if you have a document, if you have his statement, I will see what he said in the statement except that I see here that he gave this statement on the 9th of August, 2004. I have the statement here in Albanian given in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, electric shock as a method of torture by your police station is referred to in a number of sources coming independently. Do you have any comment on that? How could it be that people from different sources and in different ways complain of electric shock?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true, Mr. Prosecutor. There were no electric shocks. I still don't understand what kind of electric shocks these are. It's not true. I claim to you with full responsibility that there is no truth in that, in this kind of thing, electric shocks and electricity in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next tab, tab 14, is a statement made for the Defence in the Limaj case and produced initially to the representative of the defendant there, but can I just ask you for your assistance with this. You can have a look at the handwritten version of it if you want to. In our version it comes at the foot of page 1. This man, whose name we can see -- do you know the name, Adem Selmani?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's coming your way. You will have to cast your eyes down I think --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have his statement in the Albanian language. I see here Adem Selmani.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The title to this, Mr. Nice, doesn't suggest that it was done for the Limaj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I'm wrong -- you're quite right, it doesn't. Let me just check on that. I think -- Your Honour's quite right to observe the inconsistency. Although it came to people in the Limaj case it was made available to us in the course of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what it says, you see, and I'm afraid the handwriting isn't very easy to read, and I can't immediately find the passage --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I cannot read the handwriting although I understand the language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll read one passage, or two passages, actually from this statement. It's a man called Adem Selmani and it's at the foot of the English page 1. He says of his time at a school where he was detained in May of 1999 that when he arrived at the school you and Nebojsa Djordjevic and Sparavalo were there, that you took him, that's Adem Selmani, to classrooms and corridors. Now, is it right that you were using a school for the purposes of detaining or interviewing people in May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school was not used or a school was not used. And secondly, I did not leave my office to go to schools. I don't remember this person. I just see that he gave a statement on the 13th of May, 2005, or, rather, this statement. So obviously he could have complained to KFOR, UNMIK after we had left, and to other organisations that are in charge in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He alleges that you beat him, ordered them to sing Serb songs and to kiss this accused's picture. Did you do what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we did not beat him. Secondly, we did not make him sing Serb songs. And thirdly, I did not have the accused's picture in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second page in English of his statement he alleges that as to the Pranvera bar, which we spoke of, I think, yesterday. Do you remember the Pranvera bar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said previously that due to fear of bombing we were dislocated from the secretariat in Urosevac. So the general crime department was at the Pranvera cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means spring in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that's where we worked from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says two things about the people who were detained there. First he says that they were beaten up and electrocuted. I suppose you can just simply say that that isn't true.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true, that's not true at all. I have no idea what kind of electrocutions or electric shocks you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He goes on to say that when things got a bit dangerous you policemen would run away from the bar leaving the prisoners behind and they couldn't leave the building because it was mined. The first statement is clarified in a statement taken by Mr. Kelly - yes, by Mr. Kelly - "mined outside the building." Was that building, that Pranvera cafe, mined in order to keep people inside when you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no truth in this, Mr. Prosecutor. I never fled from my office, neither I nor my colleagues. That is total -- a total invention. What kind of a silly thing is that, that I leave people in a cafe and that I run to save my life? There is no logic in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple more points on this type of material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the third line of this statement there's a reference to a place S-h-t-i-m-e. Now, is that meant to be Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. These places frequently have alternative spellings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, was -- was use made of a school in Stimlje for police purposes of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour. I don't know if it was used, because during the NATO bombing I had not gone to Stimlje at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know the name Emin Duraku?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emin Duraku? I know there is a street by that name in Urosevac, but I don't know exactly in which part of town. Emin Duraku. There is a street by that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, if you could hand the witness the statement in his own language or in a language he understands from tab 16 and lay the English version on the overhead projector, starting, please, with the second page of the English version, which is the end of the document and then we'll come back to an earlier passage. But --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you'd like to look, please, in the document before you, which is coming your way, Mr. Jasovic, at the end of the original. This man, Avdi Hysenaj, explains that he saw you on the television testifying against KLA liberators who brought freedom to his people. He was appalled because you were the one who had tortured them and you had the courage to sit in the courtroom in order to cover up your crimes and that maybe led to his identification to the lawyers who made him available to the Prosecution to deal with. His statement, Your Honour, you'll see -- if we then come back to the first page of the statement, he says in summary about what happened to him on the 1st of February of 1999 when he was taken to Stimlje police station to begin with and then was put in a jeep and taken to Urosevac where you were said to be looking for him. So Avdi Xhevat Hysenaj, tell us about him.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this person. And what you've been saying that I worked in Stimlje, too, of course citizens of Stimlje and Urosevac know me. I don't know this person. I can't remember. If you have his statement, can you show it to me and can I have a look?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And let me see what he stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the statement that's before you. This is what he stated, and you can follow it with us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, his statement. But that he came to see me at the Secretariat of the Interior, I don't remember that and I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's see what he said. Middle of the first page. Having been taken to Urosevac where you were looking for him "they ordered to me to get in where I was originally provoked by a Serb policeman whose name was Qeda or Cedo." Do you know such a policeman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Cedo but not in Urosevac. He did not work at the police station in Urosevac. He worked at the police station in Stimlje. You can see from that what kind of statement this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. It goes on to say this: "Subsequently seven to eight policemen immediately started to beat me up without control. After a while, a policeman came from the upper floor and referred to them saying that Inspector Jasovic wanted to see me. He," that's you, "asked me why I was bleeding. I replied 'Your policemen beat me up.' He then asked me why have they beaten me up and why hadn't I admitted when I was asked. I told him I did not know what to admit. I would tell them if he knew. Jasovic told me that if he asked me questions would I have answered those. I told him I would answer if I knew anything. 'You have to answer if you want to see your children again, otherwise at 2400 hours we're going to cut your head off,' said Jasovic." Now, any recollection with this man Hardin -- I beg your pardon, Avdi Hyseni?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't remember. I never looked for this man. I could not dream of that, that he was in the ground -- on the ground floor of the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac. I cannot remember this person, really. Is there a statement of his? Then I can have a look at it and see what this person stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. Me looking for him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what he says you did. And he says that: "He told me if I wanted to live I should go to Petrove, and Laniste and bring you," Jasovic, "the KLA list and information about their weapons" or you'd kill him. You asked for KLA names of Petrove village. The witness told you that he knew nothing as he lived in Stimlje since his home had been burnt down. He didn't have any contacts with the village. You, Mr. Jasovic. Asked him who burned down his house and he explained it was burned down when the Serb forces entered the village of Petrove, and at that you became revolted. You started beating him, referring to him words such as "you asked for it" because this is not Kosovo, this is Serbia. He also on leaving -- being allowed to leave the police station had a medical certificate, although it hasn't been I think made available yet to us. What do you say about that? Did you get upset with these people, saying that this was Kosovo, not -- Serbia, not Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used words like that. Everything that he said here isn't true. And I state now, too, if that was the case why didn't he complain after we left. Because there were international representatives in Kosovo and Metohija. He could have done that. And I don't know whether this individual came to see me at all, was with me at all. If you have a document or a statement, I don't know. Probably if the individual was -- had that person been there, if he was there, if I had taken -- interviewed him, I would have made a note, and I and my colleague Mr. Sparavalo were always together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I need deal with insofar as -- I beg your pardon, there's one other tab I must deal with and it is tab 19. If we can look at that very briefly. This tab goes back to the material provided by the doctor, but it's in this form. Some of it's been summarised and indeed translated. So if Mr. Nort, if you could hand to the witness -- maybe actually on this occasion it may be easier if you bring it to me. Probably save time. Thank you very much. You understand, don't you, Mr. Jasovic, that I've turned your attention to various sources, witnesses in other cases, reports to doctors. We've looked at reports from human rights organisations, and we've started to look at the very people you say you took statements from, and they provide a picture of violence and death at your station. Now, here is a summary report prepared by the human rights organisation in Kosovo, and if the overhead projector has the first page and you have the first page, it's a summary of Serb violence against Albanian civil population during the war from the beginning of 1998 to June 1999. And as to people killed, it says that in the municipality of Ferizaj, 124 people were killed by Serbian police, army, and paramilitaries during the war. And it then goes on to say that six persons in 1998, nine persons January to March 1999, 101 persons March to June 1999, and it goes on to deal with August and into 2000. Now, do you challenge that as many as six people were killed by the police in 1998 as is summarised here? We can look at the supporting documents if we have time, but I won't do it at the moment. This is a human rights organisation preparing statistics from various source that it sets out later. Do you challenge it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do challenge it. I don't know and -- I don't really know what the answer to that question would be. I don't know how to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final point on those reports, and we don't have endless time of course, and it's this and it relates to a point I made to you earlier. The same organisation, you see, dealt with its overall area, which is the population as we can see of Ferizaj area. Population of Ferizaj and Kosovo in general have suffered --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ferizaj, Stimlje, Kacanik and Lipjan -- well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what this body records, and it says this: "I've examined these patients," he's dealing with people who have been injured in police custody in the Medicus and Dr. Xhela private clinics. That's the doctor we were talking about earlier. And the analysis includes 449 cases from the following municipalities. Then he breaks down the municipalities between Ferizaj and the other relevant municipalities within his area. And do you see what the results of the statistics coming to this human rights organisation are, that Ferizaj makes up 82.6 per cent of the complaints. Remember I said to you at an earlier part of the questioning that your police station was a particularly violent police station? This report's right, isn't it? It was a particularly violent police station.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. In addition to our area, we see the other areas, Vitia, Lipjan, Pristina. Lipjan belongs to the Pristina area, Gnjilane, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And look at the statistics of returns for those areas, ill-treatment in custody. Your police station tops the list in every conceivable way.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can't -- don't know how to answer your questions. I think superior officers would be able to answer your questions. They have the statistics. I was a crime inspector, a policeman. I really don't know how to answer these questions for Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For -- and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The statistics for Ferizaj relate to one police station or to several?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My understanding is it relates to the Ferizaj police station. Whether that includes Stimlje I'm afraid I'm not immediately alert to. But I can find out. I think -- I think it's probably the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that include Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shtima belongs to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid these places always have two names. Ferizaj is Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it one or several police stations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as we know it's one municipality and police station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Urosevac there was one police station, public police station, and for the traffic police and other police station for the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point I think is clear because four -- four entries down we're back to Stimlje, and I think that's Stimlje again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the tab number for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is tab number 19. And I've got one more question to ask on tab 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the part of tab 19 it's a sort of second block of materials or third block. I'm afraid they're not page numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Third block, page 1. With all the supporting analysis thereafter. With your leave I'll just come back to the first document I was showing him from this tab because there is one other question I should have asked him. And if he'd have the original and if the Court would be good enough on the first part of this tab to go to page 3, and if Mr. Nort would display page 3 in the English on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you, Mr. Jasovic, would go to the second page of the document you have. You'll see a block a paragraph headed 1998, which ends with these five lines: "Many political and human rights activists have been imprisoned and sentenced during the months of June and July of this year 1998. These include -- then there's Cen Dugolli, Sylejman Bytyci, Yiber Topalli, Xhavit Zariqi, Agim Recica from the LDK." And then NKMDLNJ activists Bislimi, Ferizi, Zymberi, all sentenced by the Serb installed court up to 15 years in prison, whereas Bislimi, Rexhep Bislimi, Cen Dugolli and Bilall Shala were tortured to death in Serbian prisons. And in the next paragraph dealing with murder of activists, it says: "After their imprisonment those three men, having been tortured severely and in different brutal ways by Serbian policemen and inspectors, died in prison. Bislimi, an activist, arrested on the 6th of July, died on the 21st in prison in Pristina. Cen Dugolli, arrested on the 21st of June, died on the 17th of August in prison in Pristina. Bilall Shala, arrested on the 28th of August, died 48 hours later at the Ferizaj Urosevac police station. Tortures proved by photographs that were taken after their deaths. These were murders without trial. Right. Your police station involved. What do you know about the deaths of these three men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say first here is that none of these individuals came to me for an interview. I can't say anything. I assume that these individuals, well possibly, possibly they had been for an interview in the state security sector. That's my assumption. So I can't really say anything about them. I don't know. I didn't talk to the individuals. I don't know whether they were detained or not detained, nor do I know whether they were in the Secretariat of the Interior of Urosevac at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So yet again if it's true that these police -- these deaths happened in or following custody at your police station you know absolutely nothing about it. Is that really right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in detention as you say, in custody, the room they were told in there were no deaths. Prove to me that anybody was -- died in that room, in the detention room. I think I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not necessarily in the detention room itself, Mr. Jasovic, you know this, but after the treatment they received there in your office and elsewhere or when they fell out of the window or when they were thrown out of the window, you know nothing of that, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in my office they didn't fall out of the window. In other offices I can't say. Now, you want me to tell you something about the entire secretariat, what happened in the whole secretariat. I had my line of work, so I can tell you about what I did. And I said a moment ago as well that it would be the superior officers who would be better placed to answer that question, who deal with matters of that kind. How I do know whether they were taken into custody, whether they were on the premises of the secretariat or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic we're going to turn to another topic, I think I've dealt with volume 2 of our materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I ask the Chamber to take again the binder of Racak materials. I thought I may have concluded with that but on review overnight I think there are things I ought to draw to the Court's attention and indeed to the witness's attention in our search for an account of what the Serb side said and what this witness can help us with. And I know that these ones are not tabbed with proper tabs. They're tabbed at the top. And if the Court would be good enough to go to what is marked as at the top tab 5, and I'm afraid there is -- yes, there is. There's a Serb language version for the witness. If that could be made available to the witness, please, Mr. Nort. It's at the end of -- I think Mr. Nort will need help with this, actually. Don't worry, we'll hand you the documents separately. If he can have tab 5 English on the overhead and tab 5 original for the witness. And if you'd like to go, first of all, to the last page of the English and the last page of the Serb. Now, the reason we're looking at the last page is just for this reason: The typed document or it may be a faxed document or whatever appears to be signed by someone called Janicevic but it's considerable Bogoljub Janicevic. Do you have any doubt that this is indeed your superior officer? The English is wrong. The original is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This comes from your superior officer, yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic Bogoljub at that time was the chief of -- yes, chief of the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Mr. Nort you could now come back to the beginning of this document, page -- the first page, page 1 of it. If you'd like to follow this with me, please, Mr. Jasovic. Oh. In a second. This is a document as you're reading it and we can follow it, the Judges and I, we'll wait for public display, dated the 15th of January. So the same day. What it says under the first paragraph is that measures were taken to seal off the village with a view to capturing and destroying a terrorist group. No question of arresting, detaining, or interviewing, was there? It's capturing and destroying. Right? That's the words that he uses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The word that is used in the Serbian language in this telegram from the chief of SUP is in the -- with the aim of apprehending, it says. With the aim of apprehending.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No destroying? There is no destroying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it says "and destroying" but apprehending or capturing. Mr. Nice insists on capturing and destroying. Here it says apprehending. And the liquidation of a group implies in police terms --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- apprehending.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No interpretation by the accused. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, you remember yesterday we heard from -- on the television programme Goran Radosavljevic saying how they received orders to attack to destroy terrorists and indeed he later used the word liquidate. This document, Mr. Jasovic, speaks then of capturing or apprehending and destroying a terrorist group. Did you understand that to be the purpose of this exercise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the aim of capturing and finding -- you see, the police never aims at destroying a terrorist group. It is to find them, to uncover them and capture them, the possible perpetrators of attacks and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... like that, Mr. Jasovic. Use your own brain and language, please. Let's go to the next paragraph which begins: "The battle with" --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I cannot understand that what is called for is liquidation of a terrorist group. I know that it should be uncovered and deprived of liberty, taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Liquidation means killed, doesn't it? It's quite simple.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To deprive of liberty doesn't mean to kill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Liquidation means to kill.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you? Well, let's look at the next paragraph and see if you can help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Mr. Prosecutor, you're putting me -- you're giving me a telegram, a dispatch, signed by the chief of SUP, Bogoljub Janicevic. Now, I cannot comment on his telegram. I don't know I'm a crime policeman. I cannot comment on something written by the chief of SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, the paragraph that begins starting at 0300 hours on the 15th of January, could you read the first three lines or the first sentence of that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On the 15th of January, 1999, starting at 0300 hours, measures were taken to block off the village of Racak, Stimlje municipality, with a view to capturing and destroying a terrorist group which, according to our information, had committed a number of terrorist attacks with lethal consequences in the territory of Urosevac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shall we now look at the next paragraph to assist us with our understanding of what liquidate, or "liquidirana" [phoen], I think it is, means. This paragraph reads as follows, doesn't it: "The battle with the terrorists lasted until 1530 hours. During the search of the village fire was opened at police members from a 12.7 millimetre Browning and a mortar. The terrorist group was liquidated with maximum effort on the part of the police." Liquidated meant killed, because that's what happened to them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word liquidated means liquidated, killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or to kill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph deals with the accidental -- or the injury of ricochet suffered by Bojan Trajkovic. But next paragraph, and I only draw this to attention for two reasons, one, some interest, it refers to a horseshoe ambush was applied in the blockade, and it was laid between the villages of Luznica and Rance, behind terrorist trenches and connecting trenches. During action by the unit and attempts to arrest members of the terrorist gang, so here is a reference to arrest, these fell into the ambush. "The terrorists opened fire at the same time and after some hours of fighting they were liquidated. Even though they had been called on to surrender, none of the terrorists wanted to do so." So in this paragraph we have a reference, I don't accept that it's in any sense accurate, but we have a reference to attempts to arrest, and the use the word "ambush," and the use of the word "liquidate." Does this fit with your recollection of what you were told by your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place of Luznica does not belong to the municipality of Stimlje or Urosevac. I don't know where that place is located at all. I don't know about this ambush, and I can state that I -- this is the first time I hear of it. I don't know about this operation at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then apart from the fact that we see the next sentence again begins with the word liquidate or has the word liquidate. The Court would go over to the second page in the English. And if you, Mr. Jasovic, would go over to the third page in the Serb version. We see towards the bottom of the English page and at the top of your page: "Seven persons were taken into custody to be interviewed on the issue of terrorism and were turned over for further work to the OSL of the Urosevac SUP ..." So this must be you. Terrorism, people to be interviewed, seven of them. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't say off the top of my head. How would I know who those people were? If I have a document shown me, then I could perhaps tell you, or if you know something about them or I could see in the statements, but like this I really can't say. I don't know what happened six years ago. It wasn't just one document. As I said, there were a large number of documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for me to hide who the people were if I knew who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided for the purposes of your work with any witnesses to interview as early as this day, the 16th of January? Were you? Were you provided with anyone to interview?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the date. If I were to look at the statements, perhaps, then I could tell you. But datewise, well, if I have statements linked to the date the 16th then certainly I did conduct the interviews. But if there are no statements I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember the question you've been asked before? Was there any person interviewed to give an account of how the killings actually happened? We've got this statement from the chief of police which is obviously a summary of some kind or pretend summary of some kind. Have you got any statements from any witnesses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. The chief of the secretariat here, it was a telegram by the then chief of the secretariat, a dispatch by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please tab 15 in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, were the events at Racak regarded as -- as an important stage leading to -- ultimately to the war, to the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't say, Your Honour. I couldn't answer that. I don't know how to answer that question, whether it was an important stage leading to the NATO bombing. I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you mention to me or name to me any other incident where 40 or 45 people died and you then had the opportunity to interview witnesses from the scene of the events that led to their death?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you -- well, I can't remember whether in some other incident more than 45 people were killed. As I said yesterday, I -- as for the 15th of January, 1999, I didn't come to the individuals who were eyewitnesses in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you answer my question? Can you name me another event where 40 to 45 people or a large number of people were killed and you then had an opportunity to interview the witnesses or some witnesses to that event?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of statements, I cannot remember having had information where more than 45 people were killed. On the basis of the interviews conducted with persons of Albanian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find it quite difficult to understand why you can't remember one way or the other whether you interviewed people after the events at Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked to individuals of Albanian ethnicity. I conducted interviews or information, conversations, but I said that I didn't -- for me to talk to policemen, which I didn't do, then I would need one of my superiors, a boss to tell me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not dealing with that at the moment. We're dealing with seven people who, according to this report, were taken into custody at Racak. Now, I find it difficult to see why you can't remember whether you interviewed these people or not in custody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say with full responsibility that I don't know the names of the people who were taken into custody, and I can't say off the top of my head. I'm not saying whether I did or did not. I can't remember the names of the individuals, quite simply, because it's been more than six years since that time, and I can't remember if there are statements. If you can show me statements that I conducted an interview, I would be able to tell you what the person stated in his statement, but I say with full responsibility that like this I just don't know. I can't remember. There's no need for me to hide these facts. If I did conduct an interview then I did, but I'm just saying that I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to have a normal memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the passage of time here involved has been more than six years. Now, if the persons were taken into custody, perhaps they weren't taken into custody and brought to me. Perhaps it was the state security sector that took them into custody. I just can't remember. I think my memory is normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, if I might be of assistance. May I be of assistance to you and the witness? Here in tab 1.44, there is a statement by an individual which was given on the 16th of January, for instance. Perhaps you can have a look whether that's it. The witness himself said that he took 700 statements of that kind, and you can follow the statements with their dates. They are his exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to those very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any event and for my own purposes. I don't know if the Court's looking for a moment. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to take the break now. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, before we return, I have just two or three little details I want to be sure I understand. These statements that you say were made to you voluntarily by individuals who came into the police station or were brought to the police station, is what appears in the statements what they dictated to you or is it what they said and you reformulated it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. What they stated is written in the statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's not, for example, any significant missing questions that we need to know about to understand the statements, for example, you saying, "Tell me if so-and-so was a member of the KLA"? Was there that sort of questioning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the interview, as the person is a resident of the village, was a resident of the village, we mostly asked the person about the following: Are there any members of the KLA in that village or in surrounding villages, and could the interviewee give us the names. And then in the course of interview further on we would ask whether these persons participated in the terrorist attacks and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. But the names just came out completely voluntarily in answer to the most neutral question. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not neutral questions. If the interviewee was from Racak, then I would ask, "Are there any KLA members there? Who are the members? Are there any trenches dug out, communication trenches, and so on. This is regular procedure of the organ of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you ever press any with, "But isn't so-and-so a member of the KLA?" Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, my method of work was as follows: If the interviewee gave me several names, then I would go back to establish for certain whether the names were right, whether these people were indeed members of the KLA or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second little detail. When the statement was typed up, is it your evidence that the statement was read over to the person? I think you've told us it was, but just to be sure about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every statement was dictated by me to my colleague, Mr. Momcilo Sparavalo, who typed it on the typewriter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it read to the person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was either read out or was given to the interviewee to read it himself if the person in question spoke Serbian well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they all happily signed these statements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon learning of the contents of the statement, they would sign the statement voluntarily, which in my view was normal, because these statements were taken from them without any kind of coercion. There was no extortion of statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nobody ever objected, for example, to the use of the little phrase "so-called KLA" in all the statements that you produced, did they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never came across a case where somebody objected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of course it wasn't they who said to you, "Mr. Jasovic, my son was a member of the so-called KLA," it was you who added the words "so-called," and they never objected; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never added. They themselves would use the words "the so-called KLA," the illegal organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just follow that. Every one of these Albanians whose statement says "so-called KLA" has a conversation with you where they say, "Mr. Jasovic, my son was a member of the so-called KLA." Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that we interviewed people who had been brought in, and they themselves would tell us that the so-called liberation army of Kosovo had been established, and we would have problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You need to go no further with that answer. I'm only too happy to hear you give it, and we'll move on to something else. A tiny point. Stimlje had its own police station and Racak fell within Stimlje, a police station which had a very low incidence on the records of police violence. Why was it that Racak people were interviewed and dealt with by you at your police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police station, we did not have the criminal investigation department or division. Such matters came normally under the jurisdiction of the criminal investigation division, and the Stimlje office came under the Urosevac SUP. The law on the internal affairs specifies precisely what matters come under the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the validity of your point about "so-called" may depend on how that term is used in Serbian. Maybe it doesn't have the same connotation as in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it depends on its connotation also in Albanian, not just Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed it does. I'll deal with the point if I can a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know if there is a difference, we can rely on Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there is a difference we may expect contribution from Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Contribution, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, as a policeman of some experience, you will confirm this general truth: That crooks and criminals and conspirators seeking to cover up crimes often fail to cover their tracks sufficiently, don't they, and that's how you catch them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I interviewed - I apologise - generally not criminals or prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Well, let me suggest to you, because I want it to be quite clear, I suggest to you that you, your chief, Danica Marinkovic, Goran Radosavljevic, the unnamed head of the military, Djordjevic, Sainovic, and others were and acted as common criminals in an attempt to disguise what they had done, no doubt on behalf of this accused, at Racak, but that you didn't successfully cover your tracks. I shall now explain to you why I say that. Do you understand the proposition?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, and that is not true. Except for the former chief of SUP, Mr. Bogoljub Janicevic, and Mrs. Danica Marinkovic, whom I accompanied once to conduct on-site investigation when the commander of the Kacanik police station was killed, I know these persons only officially, through official contacts. I met her on that day. Otherwise, I heard about them but I don't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
